faqs.question: Is Iceland or Norway better to visit?
faqs.answer: It depends on what you want. Iceland wins for dramatic volcanic landscapes, geothermal pools (Blue Lagoon), Northern Lights, and a genuine 'alien planet' experience. faqs.question: Which is cheaper: Iceland or Norway?
faqs.answer: Norway is significantly cheaper than Iceland. A mid-range day in Iceland costs 25,000–40,000 ISK ($180–290 USD), while a comparable day in Norway costs 1,200–1,800 NOK ($110–165 USD). faqs.question: Where is the best place to see the Northern Lights?
faqs.answer: Both Iceland and Norway (especially Tromsø) are world-class Northern Lights destinations. Iceland has the advantage of being one of the most accessible aurora destinations — you can see them from near Reykjavik on a clear night. faqs.question: Do you need a car in Iceland? What about Norway?
faqs.answer: In Iceland, a car is almost essential for independent travel — the famous Ring Road (Route 1) and most major attractions require driving. faqs.answer: Iceland: minimum 7 days to drive the Ring Road highlights (Golden Circle, South Coast, Snæfellsnes). 10–14 days lets you explore more including the Westfjords. faqs.question: Is Iceland safe for solo travel?
faqs.answer: Iceland is one of the safest countries on Earth — it consistently ranks #1 in the Global Peace Index. Crime is virtually non-existent. faqs.question: What is the best time to visit Iceland vs Norway?
faqs.answer: Iceland: June–August for midnight sun, green landscapes, accessible roads, and stable weather (though cold: 10–13°C/50–55°F). September–October for Northern Lights AND some green. November–March for deep aurora season but limited daylight and some road closures. Norway: May–June is arguably the best
